entry: Device using suction, often with agitation, to remove dirt from [[Carpet|carpets]] and hard floors. Dirt is collected in a dust bag or plastic bin. Types include stick, handheld, upright, canister and robot vacuums, and specialized shop vacuums can clean both solids and liquids. The first manual models, using bellows, were developed in the 1860s, and the first motorized designs appeared at the turn of the 20th century. In 1901 British engineer Hubert Cecil Booth and American inventor David T. Kenney independently developed suction-powered cleaners. The first portable model for the home was built in 1905 by Walter Griffiths of [[Birmingham]], England. In the United Kingdom and Ireland the appliance is often called a hoover, a genericized trademark taken from the Hoover Company, one of the first and most influential makers of the device.

Physical constant, the absolute dielectric permittivity of classical vacuum, denoted ε₀. Also called the permittivity of free space or the electric constant, it measures how dense an [[Electric field|electric field]] is permitted to form in response to [[Electric charge|electric charges]]. In [[Coulomb's law]], the constant fraction 1/(4πε₀) is approximately 9×10⁹ N⋅m²⋅C⁻². It also appears in [[Maxwell's equations]]. Its value follows from the defined [[Speed of light|speed of light]] c and the magnetic constant μ₀ through ε₀ = 1/(μ₀c²).

Device that controls electric current in a high vacuum between electrodes, also called an electron tube or thermionic valve. The first and simplest type, the diode or Fleming valve, was invented in 1904 by John Ambrose Fleming and allowed current to flow in only one direction. Adding control grids produced triodes and tetrodes that could amplify as well as rectify signals. Vacuum tubes were central to [[Radio|radio]], [[Television|television]], [[Radar|radar]] and early computers in the first half of the 20th century. From the 1940s, the invention of [[Semiconductor device|semiconductor devices]] made solid-state electronics possible, and from the mid-1960s tubes began to be replaced by the [[Transistor|transistor]]. Cathode-ray tubes remained in displays until the early 21st century. Tubes persist in some applications, such as the magnetron in [[Microwave oven|microwave ovens]], and many audio enthusiasts prefer tube amplifiers, including [[Electric guitar|electric guitar]] players.

City in Gujarat, western India, on the Vishwamitri River. Also known as Baroda, it is the administrative headquarters of Vadodara district, about 100 kilometers southeast of [[Ahmedabad]]. The name is traditionally derived from a [[Sanskrit]] term meaning "in the belly of the banyan tree"; the official name became Vadodara in 1974. Akota, now a suburb, was a trading town in the early centuries CE and a center of [[Jainism]], where a large hoard of Jain bronzes was found. Until independence in 1947, the city was the capital of the Gaekwad dynasty's princely state, and its Laxmi Vilas Palace remains a landmark. The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda is among India's premier universities. The 2011 census recorded 1,670,806 residents in the municipal corporation area.

Capital municipality of [[Liechtenstein]], on the [[Rhine]], and seat of the national parliament. The municipality had 6,108 residents at the end of 2025. Vaduz Castle, home of the reigning prince, stands on a steep hill above the town. In 1719 Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI united Vaduz and Schellenberg and raised them to a principality named Liechtenstein, after the family that had bought them. The town is the best-known in the country but not the largest; neighboring Schaan has more residents.

Elastic, muscular reproductive organ of the female genital tract, through which mammals copulate and give birth. In humans it extends from the [[Vulva|vulval vestibule]] to the [[Cervix|cervix]], the neck of the [[Uterus|uterus]]. The opening is normally partly covered by the hymen. The vagina also channels [[Menstrual cycle|menstrual]] flow. During [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]], its walls produce lubrication and friction that stimulates the [[Penis|penis]] toward ejaculation, enabling fertilization. Sexual activity can also transmit [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]], which safe sex practices can prevent. In adults the canal is typically 7 to 10 centimeters long, and its acidic environment, maintained by a microbiome dominated by *Lactobacillus* species, has a pH of approximately 3.8 to 4.5. In common speech the word is often used to mean the vulva, though the term refers to the internal structure.

Tenth cranial nerve and main nerve of the parasympathetic nervous system. Its sensory and motor fibers link the brain to organs including the heart, lungs and [[Digestion|digestive tract]], regulating heart rate, breathing and digestion. It is the longest nerve of the autonomic nervous system, and most of its fibers are sensory, carrying information from the body's organs to the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]]. It contributes to the "rest and digest" response, which calms the body after stress. An implanted vagus nerve stimulator is an FDA-approved treatment for refractory [[Epilepsy|epilepsy]].

[[Hinduism|Hindu]] tradition that regards [[Vishnu]] as the supreme being, also called Vishnuism. Its followers, called Vaishnavites, revere avatars of Vishnu, such as [[Krishna]] and [[Rama]], as incarnations of the supreme deity. The doctrine developed as regional non-Vedic cults were identified with Vishnu in the early centuries CE. Devotion to an avatar of Vishnu, often Krishna, was key to spreading the Bhakti movement across the Indian subcontinent in the 2nd millennium CE. The tradition includes four Vedanta schools, among them the Vishishtadvaita of [[Ramanuja]] and the Dvaita of Madhvacharya. Key texts include the [[Vedas]], the [[Upanishads]] and the [[Bhagavad Gita]]. A 2020 estimate by the World Religion Database counted about 399 million Hindus in the tradition, making it the largest Hindu sect.

King of [[Thailand]] since 2016, reigning as Rama X, and tenth monarch of the Chakri dynasty. Educated partly at the Royal Military College, Duntroon, in [[Canberra]], he qualified as a military fast-jet and airline pilot. He assumed the throne on the death of his father, [[Bhumibol Adulyadej]], on 13 October 2016, and was formally proclaimed on 1 December 2016. His reign has seen a marked centralization of royal power and personal wealth, and the 2020–2021 protests challenged the monarchy and Thailand's lèse-majesté laws. Estimates put his net worth at US$30 billion to US$70 billion.

Esoteric tradition of [[Mahayana]] Buddhism, also called Tantric Buddhism or Diamond Vehicle, that seeks rapid spiritual awakening through ritual and tantric practice. It emerged between the 5th and 7th centuries CE in medieval [[India]]. Practices include [[Mantra|mantras]], mudras, mandalas and the visualization of deities, including deity yoga, in which practitioners imagine themselves as enlightened beings. Teachings pass from teacher to student through initiation, and tradition holds that they descend in an unbroken lineage from the historical Buddha. The vajra, a ritual implement symbolizing indestructibility, gives the tradition its name. In [[Tibet]] it developed into Tibetan Buddhism, which became dominant in the Himalayan region and is practiced in Bhutan, Mongolia and [[Nepal]]. In [[Japan]] it shaped Shingon Buddhism, founded by [[Kūkai]].

Quantum-mechanical theory of [[Chemical bond|chemical bonding]], one of two basic theories along with [[Molecular orbital theory|molecular orbital theory]]. It describes how the atomic orbitals of separate atoms combine to form individual bonds when a molecule forms, whereas molecular orbitals cover the whole molecule. In 1916 [[Gilbert N. Lewis]] proposed that a bond forms through two shared electrons. In 1927 Walter Heitler and Fritz London used the [[Schrödinger equation|Schrödinger wave equation]] to explain the covalent bond in the hydrogen molecule. [[Linus Pauling]] then developed the concepts of resonance (1928) and orbital hybridization (1930). Valence bond theory declined from the 1960s as molecular orbital methods suited large computer programs, but it revived from the 1980s as its computational problems were largely solved.

Capital of Carabobo state in northern [[Venezuela]], the country's third-largest city and a center of industry and manufacturing. Its metropolitan region, with about 4.5 million people, is Venezuela's second largest after [[Caracas]], about 172 kilometers to the east. Captain Alonso Díaz Moreno founded the city on March 25, 1555, as the first [[Spain|Spanish]] settlement in north-central Venezuela. It became the country's capital in 1830, after Venezuela separated from [[Gran Colombia]], and was again the seat of government from 1858. The Battle of Carabobo, fought near the city on June 24, 1821, sealed independence from Spanish rule. Oil revenues and industrialization drove population growth in the 20th century. Since the mid-2010s the city's economy has contracted sharply along with the national crisis.

Capital of the Valencian Community and its namesake province, on the Mediterranean coast of [[Spain]]. It lies on the Turia River, on the east coast of the [[Iberian Peninsula]], and had a population of 841,558. Founded as a Roman colony in 138 BC, it came under the [[Visigothic Kingdom]] in the late 6th century and under Islamic rule from the 8th century. After the Aragonese conquest in 1238 it became capital of the Kingdom of Valencia. Its trade made it one of Europe's largest cities by the end of the 15th century, and it became a major [[Silk|silk]] manufacturing center in the 18th century. During the [[Spanish Civil War]] it was the provisional seat of the government from 1936 to 1937. Its port is among the busiest container ports in Europe and the Mediterranean, and the Fallas festival has been recognized by [[UNESCO]] as intangible cultural heritage since 2016. The city was European Green Capital in 2024.

Soviet cosmonaut and Russian politician, the first woman in space. Flying the solo [[Vostok programme|Vostok 6]] mission on June 16, 1963, she orbited Earth 48 times in almost three days. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo spaceflight and the youngest woman to have orbited Earth. A textile factory worker and amateur skydiver before her selection, she later served as an instructor and retired from the Air Force in 1997 as a major general. A prominent member of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union|Communist Party]], she sat in the Supreme Soviet from 1966 to 1989. Since 2011 she has served in Russia's State Duma as a member of United Russia. In 2020 she proposed lifting presidential term limits for [[Vladimir Putin]], and in 2022 she voted to recognize the breakaway of the Donetsk and Lugansk regions from Ukraine.

[[Italy|Italian]] former motorcycle road racer and nine-time [[Grand Prix motorcycle racing|Grand Prix]] World Champion, nicknamed "the Doctor." He won world titles in the 125cc and 250cc classes. Seven of his nine championships came in the premier class, including MotoGP titles with [[Honda]] in 2002 and 2003 and with Yamaha in 2004, 2005, 2008 and 2009. He holds the record of 89 premier-class victories. He retired after the 2021 season, and his number 46 was retired at the 2022 Italian Grand Prix. He owns the VR46 Racing Team and races in the FIA World Endurance Championship.

In Norse mythology, one of a host of female figures who guide the souls of dead warriors to [[Odin]]'s hall Valhalla, where the slain become *einherjar*. Valkyries bear the *einherjar* mead while they prepare for *Ragnarök*. They also appear as lovers of heroes and are sometimes described as daughters of royalty. The name derives from Old Norse *valkyrja*, meaning "chooser of the slain." Valkyries are attested in the [[Poetic Edda]] and in works by [[Snorri Sturluson]] written in the 13th century. Later works, including [[Richard Wagner]]'s opera *Der Ring des Nibelungen*, drew on them.

Indian lawyer, independence activist and statesman, known as Sardar Patel. An early lieutenant of [[Mahatma Gandhi]], he organized peasants in [[Gujarat]] in civil disobedience against the [[British Raj]] and became a senior leader of the [[Indian National Congress]]. Historians credit his 1942 speech at Bombay's Gowalia Tank with electrifying nationalists during the Quit India Movement. As India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister from 1947, he organized relief for refugees from Partition and, with [[Jawaharlal Nehru]] and Louis Mountbatten, persuaded almost every princely state to accede to India. Critics questioned the firmness of his methods, notably in [[Hyderabad]]. The [[Statue of Unity]] was dedicated to him in 2018.

Capital city of [[Malta]], the southernmost capital in Europe and the smallest in the [[European Union]], at 0.61 square kilometers. It occupies a [[Peninsula|peninsula]] between the Grand Harbour and Marsamxett Harbour. Its 16th-century buildings were constructed by the [[Knights Hospitaller]], and the city is named after Jean Parisot de Valette, the Grand Master who defended the island during the Great Siege of Malta. The city is [[Baroque]] in character, with bastions, curtains and palaces, and was designated a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 1980. Its population was 5,226 in July 2024.

Elongated low area, typically between hills or mountains, that usually contains a [[River|river]] or stream running along its length. Most valleys are formed by erosion over long periods, and river valleys are typically steep-sided and V-shaped in their upper reaches. Valleys carved by [[Glacier|glaciers]] have a U-shaped cross section. Rift valleys arise mainly from earth movements rather than erosion. In the lower valley, gradients are lowest and meanders may broaden into a [[Floodplain|floodplain]]. Some river valleys are cut so deeply that they become gorges or [[Canyon|canyons]]. The [[Grand Canyon]] in the United States is a dramatic V-shaped river valley, and Yosemite Valley is an example of glacial U-shaping.

Necropolis on the west bank of the [[Nile]] opposite Thebes, now [[Luxor]], where rock-cut tombs were excavated for [[Pharaoh|pharaohs]] and powerful nobles over nearly 500 years, from the 18th to the 20th Dynasty of the New Kingdom. It contains 65 tombs and chambers. KV5, the largest, has over 120 chambers built for sons of [[Ramesses II]]. The tombs are decorated with scenes from [[Egyptian mythology]] and reflect beliefs about the afterlife, though almost all were robbed in antiquity. The discovery of the tomb of [[Tutankhamun]] in 1922 brought the valley wide attention. It has been a [[World Heritage Site]] since 1979 as part of the Theban Necropolis.

Legendary Indian sage and poet, traditionally credited as author of the [[Ramayana]]. Revered in [[Hinduism]] as the *Adi Kavi*, or first poet, he is said to have composed the epic's first verse in grief after a hunter killed one of a pair of [[Crane (bird)|cranes]]. The Ramayana, of about 24,000 shlokas in seven cantos, tells how Prince [[Rama]] of Ayodhya's wife [[Sita]] is abducted by [[Ravana]], the demon king of Lanka. Scholars date the earliest stage of the text to between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE, with later stages up to the 3rd century CE, and no historical evidence confirms Valmiki's existence.

Seaport and naval base in Chile's Valparaíso Region, about 120 kilometers northwest of [[Santiago]]. Its commune had 284,938 residents, and its metropolitan area is the country's second most populous. The city has been headquarters of the Chilean Navy since 1817 and the seat of the National Congress since 1990. In the second half of the 19th century it was a major stopover for ships passing through the Straits of Magellan, and sailors called it "Little [[San Francisco]]." The opening of the [[Panama Canal]] in 1914 reduced ship traffic and hurt the port's economy. The historic quarter became a [[World Heritage Site]] in 2003. Today the city is also a major educational hub with several universities.

Consumption tax levied on the value added at each stage of production and distribution. Suppliers collect it from customers and remit it to the government, so it is an indirect tax, and exports are typically exempted. It is similar to a [[Sales tax|sales tax]], but under the invoice method each seller pays tax on sales and credits the tax paid on inputs, so only the difference is remitted. German industrialist Georg Wilhelm von Siemens proposed the concept in 1918. The modern form was first implemented in 1954 in France's [[Ivory Coast]] colony by Maurice Lauré of the French tax authority, and France adopted it in 1958. As of January 2025, 175 of the 193 UN member countries employed a VAT, including all [[OECD]] members except the United States.

Degree of importance of something or an action, central to [[Ethics|ethics]] and the social sciences. Values are broad preferences about appropriate courses of action or outcomes, reflecting a person's sense of right and wrong. They influence attitudes and behavior and include moral, ideological, social and aesthetic values. Personal values may agree with or diverge from prevailing [[Culture|cultural]] norms. It is debated whether values such as [[Altruism|altruism]] are intrinsic, and whether acquisitiveness should be classed as a vice or a virtue. Ethical value is sometimes equated with goodness, though goodness has more meanings. Value theory draws on [[Philosophy|philosophy]], anthropology, sociology and theology.

Device or natural object that regulates, directs or controls the flow of a fluid by opening, closing or partly obstructing passageways. Fluid flows through an open valve from higher to lower [[Pressure|pressure]]. The simplest type, the check valve, is a hinged flap that swings shut against flow in one direction. Valves may be operated by hand or automatically, driven by changes in [[Temperature|temperature]] or pressure. They are used in [[Irrigation|irrigation]], industrial processes, [[Plumbing|plumbing]] and appliances such as dishwashers and [[Washing machine|washing machines]]. Poppet valves control intake and exhaust in most internal combustion engines. In nature, one-way valves in [[Vein|veins]] and [[Heart|heart]] valves control blood flow. Sizes range from 0.1 mm to 60 cm.
